name: Anxiety Test
tagline: Check how much worry, fear and tension you have felt lately.
intro: Over the last two weeks, how often have you been bothered by the following problems? This screener includes the GAD-7, a widely used anxiety questionnaire, plus extra questions about worry, fear, physical tension, restlessness and avoidance. It takes about five minutes. It is not a diagnosis, but it can help you understand how you are doing and whether to seek support.
seoTitle: Anxiety Test: Free GAD-7 based screener
seoDescription: Do you worry a lot or feel tense? Take this 5-minute anxiety screener with the GAD-7 and get a personal report on worry, fear, tension and avoidance.

worry.name: Worry
worry.short: How often worrying thoughts have taken up your time and attention.
worry.low: Your answers suggest that worrying has not been taking over your days. You notice concerns, but you can usually set them aside and get on with things. That is a healthy balance: a little worry helps you prepare, too much drains you. Keep doing what helps you stay grounded, such as talking things through and getting enough rest. During stressful periods, notice early when your thoughts start to go round in circles.
worry.mid: Your answers suggest that worry has been bothering you on a fair number of days. Thoughts about what could go wrong may keep coming back and be hard to switch off. A simple tool is a fixed worry moment: write your worries down once a day for fifteen minutes and postpone them outside that time. Ask yourself which parts you can actually influence. If the worrying keeps growing, consider talking to your doctor.
worry.high: Your answers suggest that worry has been present most days and feels hard to control, which can be exhausting. Constant worrying is one of the core signs of generalised anxiety, and it responds well to help. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional; approaches such as cognitive behavioural therapy are effective. In the meantime, try writing your worries down and limit news and online searching for reassurance.

fear.name: Fear and panic
fear.short: How often you have felt frightened, alarmed or panicky.
fear.low: Your answers suggest that fear and panic have played a small role in your life recently. You may feel nervous in tense moments, which is a normal response, and it passes again. Your sense of safety seems fairly stable. Keep supporting it with regular rest and contact with people you trust. If you ever experience a sudden wave of panic, remember that it is unpleasant but not dangerous, and that it always passes.
fear.mid: Your answers suggest that you have felt frightened, startled or panicky on quite a few days. Your inner alarm system may be more sensitive than usual, for example during a stressful period. Slow breathing with a longer out-breath helps tell your body that it is safe. Try not to avoid every situation that scares you, because avoidance can make fear grow. If panic keeps coming back, talk to your doctor.
fear.high: Your answers suggest that fear, dread or panic have been affecting you most days. Living with that much alarm is tiring and can make the world feel smaller. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional; anxiety and panic are common and very treatable. Until then, practise slow breathing and remind yourself during a panic wave that it peaks and then passes. If you ever feel unsafe, contact your local emergency services.

body.name: Physical tension
body.short: How much anxiety has shown up in your body, for example in your heartbeat, breathing and muscles.
body.low: Your answers suggest that your body has stayed fairly calm in recent weeks. You may feel some tension during busy moments, but it does not linger. Physical signs such as a faster heartbeat are a normal part of stress and usually settle quickly. Keep supporting your body with movement, sleep and moments of rest. If tension starts to build up, notice where you hold it and give that area some attention.
body.mid: Your answers suggest that anxiety has been showing up in your body on a number of days, for example as tense muscles, a racing heart or an unsettled stomach. These signals are unpleasant but usually harmless. Regular exercise, stretching and slow breathing help your body release tension. Cut down on caffeine if you notice it makes things worse. If the physical complaints continue, mention them to your doctor.
body.high: Your answers suggest that your body has been under strong tension most days, with signals such as palpitations, breathlessness or aches. Anxiety can cause very real physical symptoms, but other causes should be ruled out, so please see your doctor or a qualified professional. They can also help you with the anxiety itself. Meanwhile, gentle movement, slow breathing and less caffeine can bring some relief.

restlessness.name: Restlessness and irritability
restlessness.short: How tense, keyed up or easily irritated you have felt.
restlessness.low: Your answers suggest that you have mostly been able to relax and stay patient recently. Moments of impatience happen to everyone, and they do not seem to dominate your days. Your ability to switch off is a real resource. Protect it by keeping time for rest and for things you enjoy. If you notice that you are becoming more irritable or restless, see it as a sign that you may need a break.
restlessness.mid: Your answers suggest that restlessness, tension or irritability have bothered you on quite a few days. You may find it hard to switch off or notice that you snap more quickly than usual. This is often a sign that your stress level has been high for a while. Plan short breaks during the day, move your body and reduce screen time in the evening. If it continues, talk to someone you trust or to your doctor.
restlessness.high: Your answers suggest that you have felt restless, on edge or irritable most days, and that relaxing has become very difficult. This can put a strain on your relationships and your sleep. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional about what you are experiencing. In the meantime, try daily physical activity, regular sleep times and a calm evening routine. Let the people close to you know that you are under pressure.

avoidance.name: Avoidance
avoidance.short: How much you have avoided situations or relied on safety habits to cope with anxiety.
avoidance.low: Your answers suggest that anxiety rarely stops you from doing what you want. You seem to face uncomfortable situations rather than steer around them, which keeps fear from growing. That is a valuable strength. Keep stretching yourself in small ways, as that builds confidence. If you ever notice that you start skipping things because of nerves, take it seriously early, because avoidance tends to grow quietly.
avoidance.mid: Your answers suggest that you sometimes avoid situations or use safety habits, such as checking or seeking reassurance, to keep anxiety down. That brings short relief but often makes the fear stronger in the long run. Choose one small situation you have been avoiding and approach it step by step. Notice that the anxiety usually drops if you stay. If avoidance keeps increasing, talk to your doctor.
avoidance.high: Your answers suggest that anxiety is clearly limiting your daily life, with many situations avoided or only faced with safety habits. That is understandable, but it can make your world smaller over time. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional; gradual, guided exposure works well for this. If you use alcohol or other substances to calm your nerves, mention that too, so you get the right support.

summary: This report combines your GAD-7 score, a widely used screening measure, with five areas that show how anxiety has been affecting you over the last two weeks. Higher scores mean more frequent problems. It is not a diagnosis; if your scores are raised, please talk to a doctor or a qualified mental health professional.

instrument.name: GAD-7 score
instrument.description: The GAD-7 is a widely used, freely available screening questionnaire for generalised anxiety, developed by Drs Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams and Löwe. Your score from 0 to 21 indicates how severe your symptoms may be, but it is a screening tool and not a diagnosis.
